p: Okay, so you mentioned that you work with the NYPD Hate Crimes Task. So how does it work? Do they refer cases to you, or is it the other way around? What? How does the flow work?
We refer cases to them.
And then they take over?
We don't have the jurisdiction to be enforcing criminal statutes, so we refer things to them.
See, okay. Thank you.

Thank you. Actually, I had a clarifying question. So a slightly different way of asking, which is– because I know– I fully trust that you guys are going to fulfill the mandate given despite all of everything. But if you could give me a sense of what the caseload looks like, and I know it varies because some of them are short-term cases and can be resolved quickly, whereas others are more complicated. But just on average, if you could give a sense of what the caseload is per person who has–
So a very high-level average is about 40 cases per person.
40 cases per— okay.

You know, again, that's not sort of reality in the sense that if someone's at trial with a very complicated case, are they also doing their other 39 cases? Probably not.

And other people are absolutely able to be banging out 60 cases at a time.
And then with the reduction in the overall budget, how is that going to change caseload per person that's working?
So again, you know, though– as I'm learning in government, there's a difference between— or there was a difference between headcount and actual physical humans in your agency.
Right.
So, we don't intend for there to be any change in people.
So, okay. So the caseload that you currently have right now was already being handled by the same number of folks that were already in positions.
And we've brought on a number of attorneys since I started successfully.
Okay. Did you want—

Oh, and because we've sort of moved, we now have a crew of non-attorney case specialists to do investigations

that'll help move attorneys off of investigations and to sort of get through their cases more effectively.
Right.

So if this is at all helpful, Chair Lee, the way the Commission used to operate was only attorneys were doing the investigative work. And so with part of the reorg and trying to use every single resource available to us, is including folks who are not attorneys into the enforcement work who will also be sharing that casework now. So now, while the average is 40 cases, we'll have more people who could have an average of 40 cases.

Right. And it's the same sort of, I guess, model as, like, community health workers or peer support navigators who can help with that work, and so that the clinical folks can do the other more clinical things that they normally do. So it seems to be the same kind of model where now you're shifting the responsibilities, which is great, because then hopefully it builds capacity. So—

And it's the same model that the Department of Labor at the federal

level and other agencies are doing to lean in. There's no reason that lawyers needed to be doing everything.
Yeah. Okay, perfect. And I'm going to pass it back to Chair Nurse.

Thank you. Just a couple questions based on your testimony. And we've talked a little bit about it in prelim in terms of the pre-complaint interventions team. How many people are on this team? How many now? How many are you looking to increase by?
Six, and we have— in the restructuring, we're increasing it by one.
It sounds so small. Okay, so you have six–
[interposing] Small but mighty.
and you're increasing by one. Okay. And I think you've talked about it before, but what are the types of complaints that are most successful when they go through this process?

So historically we primarily do physical disability access, that's like

ramps and rails and handlebars, as well as source of income discrimination. We're growing our disability access team, that's the one, the one extra. And we're also, because we are bringing on our non-attorney case specialists who will also be able to do a little bit more of the source of income work specifically, because that's, I think, amenable to people who are going to be new to the investigations, like, practice. We're trying to expand our pre-complaint intervention work to include things like pregnancy discrimination and fair chance housing and other things where early, quick, authoritative intervention can be very effective, where a phone call from the government saying you're not allowed to do this is helpful.
Okay, and then in the premeditation—
[interposing] Okay, I was wrong about the numbers. It turns out our team is eight and now it's nine.
Oh, okay, instead of six.
Yeah.
So eight, you increased by one for nine.
We have, like, our own terminology for everything, so there's, like–
[interposing] Sorry.
the precomplaint interventions team, which doesn't include our project equal access team, even though that's also pre-complaint intervention, so— sorry about that.

Totally understood. With regard to voucher holders, the pre-mediation team you mentioned normally gets complaints resolved in an average of 3.5 weeks. Are people in that period– they’re still remaining in emergency housing, or where are those folks during that time typically?

It totally depends. So the three and a half weeks is all our different kinds of early interventions, so obviously some source of income takes longer, which means that some of our other interventions are done faster. We do source of income in all different kinds, so there's people who are in emergency housing, people who are in their housing and are trying to start paying

CityFHEPS to stay, so they're still staying in that apartment. We do tell landlords that they have to hold those apartments vacant when it is someone who's looking to move into a new apartment. We put a sign on the door. We do everything that we can to make sure that that apartment remains available to them until we're done.
Okay. Just a few more questions. The new Director of Mediation role that you're looking to hire, what would the civil service title be?
It is, I believe, Executive Agency Counsel, and I will confirm that.
I think that's right.
Okay.
Yes. Executive Agency Counsel.
This is above my pay grade, understanding civil service titles.
And in the restructuring— I find that such a private sector terminology.
I know, I'm sorry.
I'm like, what do you mean?
We call it the reorg, but then it like doesn't—
When someone says it, I'm like, okay. Okay, so in that, are– is everyone keeping their civil service titles?
Yes.
Okay.

Part of what we were doing in the restructuring is we had a big a mess of civil service titles that was not equitable, where people with different civil service titles did the same job. That's really not what we want for people. It's not fair. So part of what we're doing in the restructuring is making sure that people with the same civil service titles are doing the same work, et cetera.

Okay. And then last question for the community relations experts that are being moved into more enforcement-oriented roles as non-attorney case workers or case specialists, is this similar to a paralegal role?

No, so that's a great question. So we're— so the community relations specialists, some of them are becoming the community partnership specialists. That's again deeper partnerships. Some who were doing some trainings as part of their prior job are now trainings experts. Some are becoming intake specialists and some are becoming case specialists. The case specialist really is more of a case detective. It's taking testimony under oath, it's doing discovery, it's– I mean, pre-litigation discovery, requests for information, looking through emails, looking through the whole thing, really trying to figure out and get to the bottom of the case before we decide whether to litigate the case and find probable cause or not. That's the goal. It's much– it’s a much more involved on-the-ground kind of work rather than supporting an attorney. It's really being the inner face with the

complainants and respondents as well. And part of the goal here really was to make sure, because our community relations specialists know how to talk to people and they– you know, they, like, have expertise in the industries that we're often working in, that we're bringing that expertise into case investigations rather than having lawyers who, again, not always the best at talking to people, removing them from that sort of frontline interaction where they don't need to be there.

Okay, that's going to be the end of my questions. But I just wanted to double down on what the Deputy Speaker said in terms of the appearance that we are going backwards. I know she fought really, really hard over the last four years to move the funding dial forward. And so I think perhaps, like a new organizational chart, if you could share that with the Council so we can be also a part of helping to do that ongoing assessment of how did this reorganization and restructuring create those efficiencies and how it's helping to sustain or decrease, like, wait times and things like that. I also just, you know, I loved in your

testimony that you brought dollar amounts in terms of, like, what you are able to deliver for New Yorkers. I mean, just highlighting a few— $1 million in restitution for victims of discrimination, $200,000 in civil penalties, $350,000 in damages for victims of disability discrimination, $600,000 in damages for victims of employment discrimination, from race discrimination to pregnancy discrimination to sexual harassment. I mean, this is life-changing work for people, and so if we're shortchanging this agency, I'm really, really concerned. I trust that you came in and you said, I got to take on this project of trying to find efficiencies. And I believe that you're doing it to the best of your ability. But I think that from our point of view, whenever we see such cuts and seeing that what you got, like, the second biggest decrease out of all the agencies, like, that rings alarm bells for us, particularly given the broader political context we're in and the dangers, the real dangers that people are facing. We really want to be a partner to you in making sure that we're not losing out on the gains that were

made, particularly by the former Chair here over the last four years. So that's it for me.

No, I just want to echo what the Chair just mentioned about putting dollar numbers to the savings, because I don't think a lot of people fully— because they're looking at the budget in terms of here and now. But I think what folks, and what I always try to look at is, okay, if we're investing this much now, how much will this save us as a city later in the out-years? And so I think it's important to keep that lens, which I'm glad you mentioned in your testimony. And I just, you know, I commend you on doing a lot with very little, and I appreciate that you've been able to address a lot of the concerns. And hopefully moving forward, as the Chair and Deputy Speaker mentioned, we can move forward with the budget and actually, hopefully see improvements in investments versus going backwards. So— okay. And I think that's it on our part, unless Deputy Speaker or anyone else, if you guys had more questions.
Thank you so much.
Thank you. Thank you so much.
Thank you.
Okay, so we're going to take a recess until our next hearing at 12 p.m. with Parks and Recreation. [break]
Ladies and gentlemen, please settle down. We are going to begin shortly. Please find your seats. Thank you.

Okay. Good afternoon and welcome to the second FY27 Executive Budget hearing for the day focusing on the Department of Parks and Recreation. I'm Councilmember Linda Lee, and I'm pleased to be joined by my colleague, Council Member and Chair Ty Hankerson, who's chair of the Committee on Parks and Recreation. We have been joined by our Deputy Speaker Williams, Council Member Marte, Council Member Brewer, Council Member Morano on Zoom, Council Member J. Sanchez, Council Member Narcisse, and I think that's everyone so far. Okay. So welcome, Commissioner, Tricia Shimamura and your team. Thank you all for joining us today to answer

our questions. And on May 12th, 2026, the administration released the Executive Financial Plan for fiscal '26 to 2030 with a proposed fiscal '27 budget of $124.7 billion. The Department of Parks and Recreation proposed fiscal '27 budget of $685.4 million represents less than one percent of the administration's proposed FY27 budget in the Executive Plan. And this is an increase of $31.4 million, or 4.8 percent, from the $654 million originally budgeted in the FY27 Preliminary Plan. This increase results from several actions, mostly the baselining of previous one-shots, snow removal overtime costs related to this year's blizzards, and the Wildlife Conservation Society's shortfall. As of April 26th, Parks and Recreation's headcount was 236 less than their fiscal '26 budgeted headcount for a vacancy rate of 4.6 percent. In the Council's Preliminary Budget response, we called on the Mayor to add $27.7 million to the Department of Parks and Recreation's budget to invest in critical services, including forestry management, Park rangers, stump removal, which is my personal favorite, the Green Thumb program– yay, all these are all amazing– city

park worker, park enforcement patrol. During a time where social activities are rising in costs, parks remains free to our city residents and provides a space for activities, programs, and fellowship. And as we all saw, especially during COVID, it really was a very, very important third space for our communities, and the Council remains committed to keeping such spaces free and accessible to residents. We were pleased to see that our request was partially included in the plan, with some positions being baselined, and we are grateful for that step forward. Today we would like to hear from the Commissioner about the outlook for parks employees who are still uncertain about their employment status coming July, and how we can work together to ensure that they are supported. And I now want to turn it over to my Co-chair for this hearing, Council Member Ty Hankerson, for his opening statement.

Thank you, Chair. Good afternoon and welcome to the Parks and Recreation Committee's hearing on the FY27 Executive Budget for the Department of Parks and Recreation. My name is Ty Hankerson. I am the Chair of the Parks and

Recreation Committee. I'd like to acknowledge my fellow council members who are present here today, to which they were acknowledged already. Today we will be hearing testimony from DPR on its FY27 Executive Budget, which totals $685.4 million, a decrease of $2.2 million compared to the FY26 adopted budget. While we still have not reached the one percent mark that was promised by the Mayor during his campaign, this is absolutely a step in the right direction. There is money for tree planting programs, seasonal staff and the adding more than 120 positions to the baseline. This means that more than 120 people will not have to worry about the existence of their jobs come July. But there's still work to be done to help the park staff that do not have that same luxury. While I am very happy about the baseline positions, I don't want to fail to mention the other great parts of this budget: $1.7 million for additional seasonal positions to help out during the FIFA World Cup, $3 million in baseline forestry management funding, $3.7 million for overtime to those parks workers that shoveled snow during the blizzards this year, and more than $2 million for tree planting. All great

things, but as always, there is more to be done. The FY27 preliminary budget includes $27.1 million in new needs for FY27, $6.3 million in other adjustments, and $2 million in savings. I am personally very happy to see the expansion of several parks jobs into the baseline and can't wait to see the remaining one-shots baselined as well— and can't wait to see the remaining one-shots baselined as well. One more time. And can't wait to see the remaining one-shots baselined as well. The committee is excited to hear testimony related to FY27's Executive Plan, specifically baseline one-shots, lifeguards, and concession revenue. Before we begin with testimony, I would like to thank council staff for their hard work. Our finance team, Eisha Wright, Jack Storey, Owen Kotowski [sp?], and Michael Sherman [sp?]. Our committee staff, Christopher Satori [sp?] and Patrick Mulvihil— Mulvihil [sp?], excuse me. And my own staff, my Chief of Staff Maricela Cano [sp?], and my special advisor Clive Destiny [sp?]. I will now ask the Committee Counsel to go over some procedural items and swear in the representatives from the department.

Thank you, Chair. So before we get started, just want to— as a quick reminder for this year's Executive Budget joint hearings, we're going to be doing all the public testimony on one amazing day. We're going to have a great party on June 10th. I shouldn't oversell this. Wednesday, June 10th, beginning at 9:30 a.m. We're doing all the public testimony on one day, so please remind folks in the community that they should sign up for Wednesday, June 10th for the public hearings. And now I will turn it over to Committee Counsel to swear in the witnesses for their testimony.

Good afternoon. May you all raise your hands? Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to any council member questions?
I do.
I do.
You may begin.

Great. Good afternoon, Chair Lee, Chair Hankerson, and members of the Finance Committee and Parks Committee, and other

members of the Council. My name is Tricia Shimamura, and I am pleased to be here today to testify as Commissioner of the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation regarding the agency's Executive Budget for fiscal year 2027. And to be joined today on this panel by several members of our agency's senior leadership. First, I want to recognize the Council for its continued support of our city's open spaces, and for championing the importance of parks for all New Yorkers. Thank you for the opportunity to provide an update on our agency's efforts to build and maintain a healthy and thriving park system. The arrival of warmer weather in the spring means we're heading into our peak season, when our city's green and open spaces truly come alive and more people get outdoors and take advantage of our amazing parks, beaches, pools, to lead happier and healthier lives. In the two months since we appeared before the council to discuss the Preliminary Budget, we have been busy delivering results for New Yorkers, striving for excellence in the public realm, and proving each and every day that our parks and open spaces are a crucial component to the Mayor's vision

to make this a more affordable city, because parks are for everyone. Our playgrounds are for every child. And so for the last month, we have been proud to unveil the fully reconstructed children's play area at Hamilton Fish Park in Manhattan, and the full renovation of Cuyler Gore Park in Brooklyn, and break ground on a full reconstruction of Captain Mario Fajardo Playground within Kissena Corridor Park in Queens. These projects are creating new play areas for different age groups and abilities, providing exciting new opportunities for children to explore, move, and play together. Our basketball courts are for everyone, and basketball is a lifeblood of the city. Let's go Knicks. So we were thrilled to open up— to fully open reconstructed basketball courts at Fort Four Playground in Washington's Walk in the Bronx, made possible from the support of council and mayoral funds. We also unveiled the newly reconstructed Grant Park also in the Bronx, a $17 million capital project made possible through the Jerome Avenue rezoning initiative, conforming a former roadbed and unused lots into 4.7 acres of park with an open lawn area, basketball court, and other

amenities. Our cultural institutions, just like our— including our city's incredible botanical gardens, are for everyone. So we recently completed a $4 million project to transform the pedestrian overpass over the Bronx River Parkway, connecting Bronx Park East residents to the New York Botanical Gardens, one of the most— world's most distinguished botanical gardens and a New York City cultural treasure. Our city waterways and shorelines are for everyone, and they are critical for the health and safety of New Yorkers and marine wildlife alike. So our Office of Marine Debris Disposal and Vessel Surrendering has been keeping our city waterways clear with marine hazard— of marine hazards. We have just announced the expansion of our Marine Vessel Turn-in program so we can take in vessels that owners can no longer take care for before they become derelict, building on the great progress we've already made in cleaning up over 120 derelict vessels clogging our waterways. Our public art is for everyone, so we unveiled for the first time a new permanent commemorative public artwork in a New York City park in over five years, installed in Elizabeth H. Berger Plaza in Manhattan

to celebrate the literary legacy of New York's first Arabic-speaking community and shine a light on an often-forgotten facet of our city's diverse history. Our urban forest is for everyone, and it serves as an essential living infrastructure to keep our city cool and resilient. So we were proud to stand alongside the Mayor's Office of Climate and Environmental Justice, and other partners to announce the city's first-ever urban forest plan, a comprehensive roadmap to preserve our tree canopy, plant more trees, and cultivate an ecosystem of stewardship. The plan laid out the city's goal of achieving 30 percent canopy by 2040 so that every New Yorker can enjoy the vital benefits that trees provide— advancing environmental justice, mitigating heat impacts, and improving our quality of life. Our recreation centers are for everyone, so we have been extremely gratified to see how quickly the local community has embraced the newly opened Shirley Chisholm Recreation Center in East Flatbush, Brooklyn, where we have already enrolled over 11,000 new members. Later this year, we look forward to opening the brand new Mary Cali Dalton Recreation Center in Staten Island, as well as

reopening well-loved recreation centers after extensive and much-needed renovations, including Lost Battalion Hall in Queens, Owen Dolen Recreation Center and St. Mary's Recreation Center in the Bronx, and Sunset Park Recreation Center in Brooklyn. Last but not least, our city's swimming beaches are for everyone. Though the weather was not quite what any of us had hoped for this Memorial Day, it was still a great start to the season, as we opened up all of our public beaches for swimming. Our tireless maintenance and operations staff are out in full force keeping our beaches and boardwalks clean, and our dedicated Parks Enforcement Patrol officers are keeping swimmers and beachgoers safe, as are our incredible beach lifeguards. We are pleased to report that over the weekend, the agency's active lifeguard corps currently stands at 370, a significant increase over this point in time last year. As we continue to train and certify additional new and returning lifeguards our staffing levels will increase, typically reaching their peak around the 4th of July after our outdoor pools have opened, and we hope to ultimately exceed last year's staffing peak of 1,082 lifeguards

citywide. We were especially thrilled to reopen the beautiful and historic Orchard Beach Pavilion to the public for the first time since 2009. This $114 million reconstruction project advanced in partnership with the New York City Economic Development Corporation, restored the historic architecture of the landmark building, providing greater ADA accessibility, and revamped concession and community spaces, enhancing the visitor experience. We are proud to have restored the Pavilion to its historic glory, with a level of investment that properly reflects this incredible beach's place in the hearts of Bronxites and all New Yorkers. Turning to the specific topic for this hearing. The fiscal year 2027 Executive Budget reflects the administration's ongoing commitment to fiscal responsibility amid economic and fiscal challenges facing the city while maintaining critical services for all New Yorkers and investing in a greener, healthier city. The operating budget for our agency in the FY27 executive budget is $685.4 million, a $31.4 million increase from the Preliminary Budget, reflecting the addition of a

significant new needs expense funding, including, as you mentioned, the $15 million in baseline funding for what was known as one-shot funded staff lines in our natural forest management, maintenance and operations, and ranger divisions. The first time in recent memory that this funding, typically provided once— one fiscal year at a time, has been mayorally baselined before budget adoption. The FY27 Executive Plan also provides new funding for continuation of our in-house tree planting program— pilot program, so we can continue exploring ways to more efficiently green our city and grow our tree canopy, as well as an expansion of our seasonal staffing plan to support increased park usage during the summer's World Cup, Sail 4th 250, and Sail 4th 250 festivities. Our agency's 10-year capital plan is $12.1 billion, including over $93 million in new additional funding to complete necessary repairs on park bridges around the city, which will be managed by our sister agency partners at New York City Department of Transportation. Though I am still new in my tenure leading this agency, I could not be prouder of the dedicated parkies that give their all to make our

park system the very best it can be. And I could not be more excited about this coming summer. I'll end my testimony with a short history lesson. In the summer of 1936, 90 years ago, New York City held a series of opening ceremonies for 11 new gorgeous outdoor pools funded and constructed by the WPA, or Work Progress Administration, a New Deal agency that employed millions of Americans during the depths of the Great Depression, lifting families out of poverty while delivering sorely needed public infrastructure projects to underserved neighborhoods. These 11 majestic pools are still beloved and enjoyed by local New Yorkers, but they stand also as a testament to what government can achieve when it marshals in the political will and resources to deliver for its constituents, a level of commitment that our agency strives to honor and embody every single day. We're going to be celebrating this historic anniversary in some very fun and unique ways as our outdoor pool season kicks off later this June. So please stay tuned for more details, as I hope you all can join us and enjoy some fun in the sun this summer. I want to thank the Council for its support in improving our

parks and open spaces for all New Yorkers, and for the opportunity to testify today. We'd now be happy to answer any questions that you may have.

Great. Thank you, Commissioner. Alright, so let's just get right into things. By the way, I did— actually, I'll tell you that story later. For one-shots, I, as well as I know the Chair, have always hated that there were hundreds of people working at the Parks Department that have their jobs as one-shots, and it's very hard to plan, budget, all of the things that we need to do, hiring, which takes a long time in and of itself. So we know there's a lot of challenges around the one-shot funding. So— In terms of the city park workers and rangers, I know that those were the ones that I believe were not baselined. And so— oh wait, sorry, those are the ones that were baselined, sorry.
Those are.

While the parks enforcement patrol positions were not. And so just wanted to get some insight if you had, you know, insight with your conversations with OMB or the Mayor's office as to why those were not included.

Yeah, you know, first and foremost, I want to just lay the groundwork and say that we all understand that this was an incredibly difficult budget year, that this administration was really focused on delivering a budget that was transparent and fair and balanced. Most importantly, we knew that as an agency, we also played a role in this. So I want to recognize, first our team that worked directly with OMB that continues to work directly with OMB every day to talk about the needs of the agency, but also kind of our role in overall delivering a balanced budget. Right– I also want to recognize that $15 million baselined is truly something that has not happened under an Executive Budget in, in anyone's actual memory here, and parkies go back a ways. And so the idea that the Mayor would— and this administration would step up to baseline these items prior to adoption of a final budget is really exciting. But certainly I think that it was about just overall delivering on a kind of full picture of what was allowed and what could— what could be— happen in this budget. And we're very excited to see– you mentioned the Rangers. This is

over 50 percent of our Ranger program– was in one-shot funding. To have that baselined is game-changing when it comes to this division. Our maintenance workers, we know how important every single maintenance and operations staff member is. I cannot emphasize that enough. So to have 73 additional staffers who are included in our ranks fully, is absolutely fantastic news. And we know very much the significance of the other divisions— PEP, Parks Enforcement Patrol, Green Thumb, and others. So that's– you know, I would argue– I can argue all day that every single component of my agency is value added.

And then in terms of– but just going back to the PEP, you know, the Parks Enforcement Patrol. In the conversations you're having, does it sound promising that hopefully those things will get baselined, or, you know, if not, then I guess we have to go through usual process.

Yeah, you know, I think, like– our relationship with OMB has never— has arguably never been better. We're very grateful. I think that we hear a lot from the administration, are

in regular conversations around the significance of all the divisions, particularly the ones that are still one-shot funded. And so we're having regular, if not daily, if not twice a day conversations at this point around what are— what the these units are bringing to our park system and how incredibly valuable they are.

Okay, perfect. And then in terms of the previous– I know previously the ranger one-shots were $4.1 million per year, and when they were baselined this year, the total cost was $5.8 for the same level of headcount. So just wanted to know if you could let us know what the delta of that is caused by.

Sure. I'm going to probably defer to our Executive Financial Officer to talk about that shift, but I believe that this is really just, like, the same amount of Rangers, that this is just an increase in their overall benefits–
[interposing] Cost of living?
and kind of lines there. But go ahead, David, if you'd like to add any more to that.
Well, if I don't have to tell the truth or— okay. So– yeah, so OMB added that money. There's a heavy costs associated with both Rangers and PEPs for bulletproof vests—
Hold on one second, you have to be sworn in. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before the committee and to respond honestly to councilmember questions?
Yes, no, I will.
Now you may go.

Okay. Yeah, there's additional costs associated beyond the cost of the individuals for bulletproof vests and equipment that they have, and it's very heavy. So they've actually increased that so we can cover those costs. And it was very—
[interposing] I see. Okay. So it's not just the personnel, it's also OTPS as well.
Yes.

Okay. Got it. Perfect. Thank you. And is there any budget limitation for why PEP officers cannot be baselined from the best of your knowledge, or is this, you know, something that could be included in that? Just wanted to get clarification in the baseline. So there's nothing, I guess, legally, logistically, or whatever that would prevent them from— okay, perfect. Okay. Now sort of adjusting a little bit to tree planting. I'd like to sort of— the plan included a new need of $2.1 million and 19 positions for tree planting. So would you be able to break down how this money will be spent, and how many tree plantings will this support?

Yeah, it's a great question. So to actually provide clarity here, the positions that were funded in the Executive Budget were for forestry management, which— oh, is that— oh, in the in-house pilot. I'm sorry. Yeah. So the— sorry. So, we've been running an in-house tree

planting pilot for at least the last year, if not a little bit longer. This was done for a number of a number of reasons. We are always paying very close attention to the overall kind of industry of contractors, of work that's out there, the cost of these contracts, kind of the ebbs and flows of the tree planting industry. And we're seeing a kind of overall kind of uptick year after year of kind of higher costs associated with tree planting. I just— under the last two years, we decided to undertake our own in-house tree planting pilot program to see if we could do this work ourselves in-house. It's been going very well. We've focused predominantly on– in Queens Village with this, which is as an– yes, this. And it's been going very well. So we're very excited to have again this, another year of this pilot to continue to see how our running our own operation in-house really impacts the overall market. Yeah, would love to hear more about that. And if it's more efficient,–
[interposing] Sure.
if you're finding that there's less red tape to go through.
I'm actually gonna ask our Assistant Commissioner Ben Osborne–
[interposing] Sure.

for Forestry to come up just to see, make sure I didn't say anything incorrectly, but also to see if he would like to add anything about how the pilot's been going since it's been a year and we're very excited to see it undergo another year.
Yes, good morning.
You may have to swear.
Yes, I'm ready to be sworn in. Thanks.
Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this to respond honestly to councilmember questions?
Yes, I do.
You may begin.

Okay, thank you, Commissioner, and thank you, council Member, for the question and the interest in our in-house tree planting program. So as the Commissioner noted, we began planning for this in-house tree planting program during a time when we were seeing contractor costs increasing, and we wanted an alternative to contracted tree planting, partly as a way to control costs. In the intervening years while we've been working out this plan, we've actually managed to stabilize and in fact reduce our contracted tree planting costs, which we're very proud of. But we're also really happy with the initial success of this in-house tree planting program. To date, this team which has consisted of 13 people, so far has planted over 1,800 trees in Queens Village, which is a high-HVI neighborhood. With this additional funding, which will— the funding is for the headcount as well as associated OTPS. We're going to be increasing the number of personnel on the team, which will hopefully increase the number of trees
